candidates.raw_excerpt: Apple hasn’t exactly impressed with its AI offerings. And privacy-minded Mac users were even less compelled by the company’s decision, with macOS 27, to remove a setting that allowed you to disable and delete its Apple Intelligence features. But never count an annoyed userbase out. As spotted by MacRumors , someone’s created a new open-source tool that allows Mac users to nuke every trace of Apple’s borderline useless AI models from their machines — and it’s already making waves in the Mac community. The tool, called RemoveMacAI, disables Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, and the ChatGPT Extension, the developer explained in a r/MacOS post that’s received over a thousand upvotes. To ensure you keep living a blissful AI-free existence, the tool also prevents the Intelligence features from ever being downloaded again, the developer claims. candidates.title: Hot Take: How technology helps a city act before complaints arrive
candidates.raw_excerpt:
How can a city hear its people before they even speak? In Beijing, the answer starts with a phone number: 12345.

Over the past seven years, this hotline has handled 180 million requests from residents and businesses, with resolution and satisfaction rates both above 97%. But the real story is not just the calls that come in. It is what technology does with the information.

Every day, AI-powered systems sift through the data, grouping complaints by keyword, location and urgency and generating heat maps that show where the city is struggling. Analysts use these patterns to anticipate emerging problems: which neighborhoods repeatedly experience issues, which disputes peak in certain months and which types of complaints arrive in waves.

A single case tells you little; the data can reveal much more. For example, if elevator complaints in one district keep climbing, maintenance or renewal needs may be mounting.

The data does not just record the past. It points to the future.

This is where "One Topic a Month" begins.

Every month, algorithms identify a high-frequency problem in the data and bring it to the attention of a municipal department. Three levels of government work together. The goal is not to resolve a single case, but to address an entire category of problems.

Yet technology alone cannot govern a city.

Volunteer "lane managers" walk the alleys, spotting problems before they grow. Residents, businesses and community workers all become part of the early-warning system, providing eyes and ears that no algorithm can replace.

The result is a city that no longer waits for the phone to ring.

candidates.title: Astrolight Delivers Space-to-Ground Laser Communications Links
candidates.raw_excerpt: Astrolight has reached a key technology milestone as it looks to bring laser communications more into the satellite mainstream. For the first time, it established end-to-end optical communication links from its ATLAS-1 laser communication terminal in orbit to its OGS-2.5 optical ground station in Greece. Astrolight announced the demonstration on Oct. 8, in which the link moved from first light to routine operations at 1 Gbps within a week. The company developed the terminal working with the European Space Agency and worked with the Department of Aerospace of the University of Athens, and the Department of Physics of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki on this project. In the demonstration, Astrolight’s ATLAS-1 laser communication terminal on the ERMIS-3 a nanosatellite connected with the with HolOGS-1 optical ground station in Holomondas, Greece. Astrolight upgraded the ground station to its OGS-2.5 model for the PeakSat mission. Astrolight’s team in Lithuania has operated both systems remotely. The company reports that ATLAS-1 is currently transmitting data at 1 Gbps, while link budget margins indicate that the system could support rates of up to 10 Gbps. Both ATLAS-1 and OGS-2.5 achieved first light during the satellite’s first active pass over the ground station. The systems operated autonomously on a pre-scheduled basis at both ends of the link by the third pass. “The next step for laser communications is making them routine for satellite operators, with high-capacity links that can be deployed and operated remotely with minimal operational oversight. Proving that our space and ground systems have this capability brings us closer to making optical connectivity practical for commercial missions at scale,” Dalius Petrulionis, CTO and co-founder of Astrolight, said in a statement. candidates.title: L3Harris to Build Telescope for ESA’s LISA Mission
candidates.raw_excerpt: L3Harris will build an all-glass telescope for the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission expected to launch in the mid-2030s. The European Space Agency (ESA) is leading the mission, with NASA as a collaborative partner. NASA awarded L3Harris the contract this week. NASA is contributing the telescopes and other critical hardware as well as engineering and scientific support. LISA will be the first gravitational wave detector in space. It is designed to detect gravitational waves in space by measuring distance changes between satellites using laser beams. This will inform the study of black holes, colliding stars, and space-time. It is designed as a constellation of three spacecraft. L3Harris said that each satellite will include two L3Harris telescopes capable of transmitting and receiving precision laser beams with the support of ceramic glass. The company has manufactured a full-scale prototype for the mission. “LISA will open a new window into the universe that ground-based observatories cannot access,” said Jeff Hanke, president of Space Systems, Space & Mission Systems for L3Harris. “By listening to the low-frequency ripples in space-time across millions of kilometers, LISA allows the study of massive, distant and rare cosmic events that are otherwise invisible.” ESA recently selected Germany’s OHB, together with Thales Alenia Space to build the three-spacecraft mission. candidates.raw_excerpt: For anybody who thought AI companies were about to unlock trillions of dollars in profits, OpenAI has bad news for you: it ain’t happening anytime soon. Some red-hot reporting from the Financial Times just revealed that OpenAI’s annualized revenue — an estimated guess at a company’s income for the year — is roughly $20 billion lower than anybody had previously expected, including, it seems, OpenAI itself. Because OpenAI is a private company, it’s important to note that we don’t know for sure what’s going on under the hood. That said, the FT based its reporting on internal memos to investors issued in late September. Basically, the AI lab told backers to expect revenues approaching $50 billion — far shorter than the explosive $70 billion number reported previously. Though that $70 billion figure was also based on leaked investor memos, OpenAI wasn’t in any hurry to deny it, digging itself into a $20 billion hole. Given the monumental difference between those two figures, investors across the world of finance are taking it as a sign that demand for AI is much lower than previously thought — a signal with ripple effects that extend far beyond OpenAI. At the closing bells on Wall Street on Thursday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down a whopping 1.25 percent on the day, while the S&P 500 fell by 0.47 percent. Particularly hard hit were companies sandwiched in the middle of the AI supply-chain, like the chipmaker Nvidia, which tumbled by nearly 3 percent following the news from the FT . All of this comes a week after consulting firm Bain and Co issued a gloomy report finding that the global AI industry would have to reach annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 to justify the amount of spending on AI data centers — a formidable summit, which is now $20 billion farther after the latest disclosures. The guidelines outline 19 key measures in five areas of innovation, including advancing scientific and technological innovation, deepening the integration of sci-tech and industrial innovation, innovating development approaches, promoting institutional and mechanism innovation, and improving mechanisms for talent development.

candidates.title: China's FAST telescope finds rare triple-star system still evolving
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese astronomers have found a rare evolving triple-star system involving a pulsar, using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST). 

The system, called J0435+3233, gives astronomers a natural lab to study how stars evolve and pull on each other, and test fundamental theories of gravity, including the strong equivalence principle. Its discovery also shows the value of combining observations across different wavelengths. The findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Friday.

Scientists believe all three stars formed from the same cloud of gas and dust. The heaviest exploded and became the pulsar. The second evolved into a white dwarf. The lightest survived both stages and is still evolving. Eventually, it too will become a white dwarf, leaving a stable system with one pulsar and two white dwarfs.

A pulsar is a fast-spinning neutron star that fires beams of radio waves. Analyzing five years of FAST observations, scientists found this one spins once every 3.2 milliseconds and orbits a white dwarf – the dense core of a dead star – once every eight days.

Researchers combined the radio data with publicly available infrared, optical and gamma-ray data to identify a third star, with a mass similar to the Sun's. It orbits the inner pulsar-white dwarf binary once every 73.5 years on an elongated path.

The third star also explains a strange FAST reading: the pulsar's spin period is increasing by about one nanosecond a year, roughly 100 times faster than comparable pulsars. The pull of the distant companion is behind this change.

The projects will generate carbon credits aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Under Singapore's International Carbon Credit Framework, the credits may qualify for use by Singapore-based companies liable for carbon tax to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions.

Interested parties may apply for authorization of eligible carbon credit projects in Mongolia. The two governments will review applications jointly on a rolling basis.

The agreement is Singapore's sixth bilateral implementation agreement under which Singapore has opened applications for carbon credit projects, following similar agreements with Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda and Thailand.

candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX announced a deal Thursday afternoon to acquire nationwide, low-band spectrum from Grain Management to improve service for Starlink Mobile and enable the service to operate indoors. SpaceX and Grain Management said SpaceX will acquire 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band. The deal is subject to FCC approval. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. This comes just after the FCC approved SpaceX to deploy 15,000 satellites for its Starlink Mobile direct-to-device constellation. SpaceX explained how this spectrum will complement the service in a statement: “While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings,” SpaceX said. Grain is a private investment firm that acquired the block of spectrum from T-Mobile in a deal announced in early 2025 and just completed in August for $2.9 billion in cash and additional spectrum licenses. The spectrum’s “propagation characteristics make it well-suited for a broad range of mission-critical applications, including private wireless networks for electric utilities and other critical infrastructure operators, enterprise communications, and next-generation direct-to-device (D2D) satellite services,” Grain said in a recent statement. SpaceX also stated that most existing mobile devices already support this spectrum band. With this spectrum and the second-generation of Starlink Mobile satellites, SpaceX said Starlink Mobile will be “the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum,” and the network will provide “reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.” Starlink Mobile, the direct-to-device constellation, is separate from SpaceX’s broadband internet constellation.

candidates.title: Don’t Want to Spend Time With Your Kids? Train an AI Voice Model of Yourself to Read Them Bedtime Stories
candidates.raw_excerpt: Parenting is hard. Why not let an AI model take over some of your childrearing duties? It may come at the expense of forming lasting emotional bonds with your progeny, but that’s a tradeoff that some AI adherents, evidently, have calculated to be worth it. OpenAI Sam Altman has bragged about how much he relies on ChatGPT to raise his son, and also thinks it’s a good idea to let an AI-generated podcast replace the “so how’d your day go?” catchup talk a mom or dad has in the car when they pick their kid up from school. Altman’s comments were ruthlessly — and rightfully — mocked at the time. But his robo-rearing ideas pale in comparison to this latest take from an AI bro. In a now deleted post on X, Alvin Sng, a software engineer at the startup Factory AI, recalled a conversation he had with his wife when she asked him to read his newborn baby a book. As he explained, he had a better idea that required zero effort on his part. “I can just play an audiobook from my phone,” he told her. His spouse reasonably complained that an audiobook wouldn’t be in his voice. But Sng wasn’t to be outdone in the zero-effort-parenting department. “I can train a voice model,” he countered, before addressing his readers: “Parenting hits different when you work in AI.” Folks, what is the p(doom) of becoming estranged from your kid? A baby can’t understand what a father is reading it, but it can recognize his voice. There’s something perverse about some of a baby’s early and formative exposure to what its father sounds like being an AI approximation. And already wanting to automate parenting duties this early on doesn’t bode well for the future. The precious time between a child and a parent doesn’t need to be streamlined, but the AI industry is obsessed with selling us on the idea of optimizing every part of our lives. Let an AI like Meta’s buzzy Muse agent send texts and emails on your behalf. Let an AI plan out your day or plan out your vacation. Let it handle bookings and reservations.

candidates.title: Amazon builds 1,000th satellite, will launch space internet service by end of year
candidates.raw_excerpt: The world's largest retailer wants to sell you something else—Internet from space. Amazon has been developing a constellation of satellites to deliver broadband Internet from low-Earth orbit for the better part of a decade, and the company is just about ready to pull back the curtain. It is entering a market that SpaceX, with its Starlink Internet, has dominated for the last half-decade. Amazon's debut into satellite Internet is being closely watched, not just by some consumers, but by businesses ranging from airlines to shipping companies to governments. Broadband Internet from orbit has proven broadly useful for a lot of purposes, from video games to commerce to warfighting. But until now, most people had to buy it from Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb has only offered limited services, leaving Amazon as the only real competitor to deliver high-speed Internet globally. Moreover, at the head of the company's broadband efforts is Rajeev Badyal, who led Starlink during its early years, but whom Musk fired eight years ago for moving too cautiously on Starlink. candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: The Exploration Company The Exploration Company has announced it will test a lunar hopper demonstrator called ONEIROS in the United Arab Emirates in 2027. ONEIROS is a privately funded initiative focused on validating technologies that could eventually support lower-cost access to the lunar surface. The company plans to build a one-tonne demonstrator that will use a throttleable methane-fuelled rocket engine, autonomous navigation, and hazard-avoidance systems to demonstrate the capabilities needed for controlled landings on the Moon. According to the abstract of a paper presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye, work on the project began earlier this year. Teams have already built several breadboards to reduce technical risks ahead of the planned flight demonstration next year. The decision to conduct the flight demonstration in the UAE follows a memorandum of understanding signed with the country’s national space agency to support the project and develop local testing capabilities. While no subsequent binding agreement has been announced, the abstract confirmed that testing would take place in “the UAE desert.” The Exploration Company intends to follow ONEIROS with Hilal, a demonstrator designed to validate precision landing capabilities and methane/oxygen propulsion technologies on the Moon’s surface. Following that, the company told European Spaceflight that it would take “step-by-step approach to lunar vehicle development.” Beyond its lunar lander programmes, The Exploration Company is also part of a consortium selected by the European Space Agency in February 2026 to conduct a Lunar Remote Camp study . Led by the Danish firm SAGA Space Architects, the consortium is developing a concept for a deployable lunar shelter that would initially support robotic operations, with the potential to accommodate astronauts during short stays on the lunar surface. candidates.title: Finland Orders Google to Suspend New Data Centers After Contractors Pave Over Protected Forests
candidates.raw_excerpt: Finish environmental authorities are in a rage over Google’s $15 billion data center projects after the discovery that company contractors had chopped down some 330 hectares of government-protected forests, seemingly without a permit. According to Agence France-Presse , the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) demanded that the Google-affiliate company Tuike Finland Oy “immediately suspend… all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment” in connection with two planned data center developments in the Northern municipalities of Muhos and Kajaani. In all, LVV accuses Google’s contractor of clear-cutting some 330 hectares in Muhos without completing a mandatory environmental impact assessment, a necessary step for receiving approval. The company cleared a further 200 hectares for its data center in Kajaani, though it isn’t clear whether that logging was approved by authorities. As the Guardian reported , Google has just over a week to explain its actions to Finnish officials. Though a government review is only just getting underway, the tech giant is already expressing remorse. In a statement to AFP , Google spokesperson Sondre Ronander admitted the company messed up, saying “we understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance.” “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance,” Ronander continued. As head of the environmental department of the LVV Tommi Muilu told AFP , Google has not only felled hundreds of acres of trees, but has stripped topsoil, engineered roads and storage areas, and altered ditches. Speaking to AFP , chair of the long-running Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said Google had paved over “nature sites which should be preserved.” More on data centers: Amazon Warns Local Communities to Stop Defying Its Massive AI Data Centers The post Finland Orders Google to Suspend New Data Centers After Contractors Pave Over Protected Forests appeared first on Futurism .

candidates.title: ArianeGroup Completes Second Themis Wet Dress Rehearsal
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ArianeGroup / SSC Space The European Space Agency announced that ArianeGroup and SSC Space completed a second wet dress rehearsal of the Themis reusable rocket demonstrator at Esrange in Sweden. ESA announced the completion of the latest rehearsal on 7 October, saying that the test had taken place on 29 September. As with the first wet dress rehearsal , completed in July, the demonstrator was filled with liquid nitrogen rather than propellant. The nitrogen was cooled to around -200°C, allowing teams to test the vehicle and ground infrastructure under similar cryogenic temperatures and pressures without the added risk of propellant loading. The second rehearsal also included tests of elements of the automated ground systems developed to support reusable operations. After the demonstrator touches down following a test, robotic systems are expected to locate the vehicle, connect to it, and drain any remaining fuel and oxidiser while personnel remain at a safe distance. Previously, ESA said a hot-fire test of the demonstrator’s Prometheus engine would follow a full wet dress rehearsal using liquid oxygen and liquid methane. As a result, unless the test sequence has since changed, at least one further rehearsal will be conducted before teams progress to a hot-fire test. According to a statement from the SALTO consortium, “teams are now working on defining a window for the next test.” The consortium is conducting the initial Themis flight campaign under the European Union-funded SALTO initiative. The €42.8-million project is funding the first two low-altitude hop tests of Themis to demonstrate that the vehicle can be launched, recovered, and then launched again. During the first of those flights, Themis is expected to climb to an altitude of up to 100 metres before descending and attempting a vertical landing.
